title: When minun and sinun can be left out
summary: Omit minun or sinun while retaining the ending; keep hänen in identification sentences.
targetSkills: Possessive pronoun omission and clear reference
prerequisiteSkills: Plural possessed nouns in ownership sentences
objectives: Omit minun or sinun while retaining the ending; keep hänen in identification sentences.
Apply this rule with the supporting forms shown.

sections.title: How the pattern works
paragraphs: Minun and sinun can be left out because their endings already identify the owner. Keep the noun ending: “Tämä on minun palloni.” and “Tämä on palloni.” have the same ownership meaning.
This also applies to several things: “Nämä ovat sinun kirjasi.” and “Nämä ovat kirjasi.” mean “These are your books.”.
In these identification sentences retain hänen: its shared third-person ending does not identify the intended owner by itself. Third-person omission in other sentence structures is outside this pack.
A task requesting omission requires omission. A task requesting the owner pronoun requires it. Otherwise ordinary first-/second-person answers accept both forms.
keyPoints: Omit minun or sinun while retaining the ending; keep hänen in identification sentences.

steps: Tämä on (“This is”) identifies one thing.
pallo (“ball”) + -ni = palloni.
The ending identifies the owner, so omit minun while retaining the noun ending.
Tämä on (“This is”) identifies one thing.
kirja (“book”) + -si = kirjasi.
The ending identifies the owner, so omit sinun while retaining the noun ending.
Nämä ovat (“These are”) identifies several things.
autot (“cars”) drops plural -t before -ni: autoni.
The ending identifies the owner, so omit minun while retaining the noun ending.
Nämä ovat (“These are”) identifies several things.
kynät (“pens”) drops plural -t before -si: kynäsi.
The ending identifies the owner, so omit sinun while retaining the noun ending.
Tämä on (“This is”) identifies one thing.
tyyny (“pillow”) + -nsä = tyynynsä.
Hänen (“his”) selects the owner ending -nsä.
Retain hänen in this identification pattern so the owner stays clear.
Nämä ovat (“These are”) identifies several things.
pelit (“games”) drops plural -t before -nsä: pelinsä.
Hänen (“his”) selects the owner ending -nsä.
Retain hänen in this identification pattern so the owner stays clear.

commonMistakes: Omitting the owner pronoun does not remove its noun ending.
Retain hänen in this bounded identification pattern.

practiceExercises.prompt: Optional practice: Write “These are my pillows.” in Finnish. Begin with Nämä ovat. Leave out minun; keep the noun ending. Use tyyny (“pillow”).
practiceExercises.explanation: Nämä ovat identifies several things. The ending -ni identifies my ownership. Minun can be omitted because the ending identifies the owner; the suffix stays.

sentenceExplanation.pattern: demonstrative + agreeing olla + optional owner pronoun + possessed noun

parts.formation: Nämä is the plural of tämä: several things.
Use ovat with several things, independently of how many people own them.
tyynyt (“pillows”) loses its plural -t before -ni: tyyny + -ni = tyynyni. The ending identifies the owner, so minun can be left out.

answerDiagnostics.explanation: Drop the noun’s plural -t before -ni: use tyynyni.
Keep the possessive ending -ni even when the owner pronoun is present or omitted.
Minun needs -ni; changing the ending changes the owner.
These are several things: Nämä needs ovat, regardless of the number of owners.

practiceExercises.explanation: Nämä ovat identifies several things. The ending -si identifies your ownership. Sinun can be omitted because the ending identifies the owner; the suffix stays.
